checks.claim: Bolt rule of thumb: a simple hardware product costs $100k-$500k and takes ~6-9 months to develop; complex products cost millions and take years (lens attributes it to 'Hardware by the Numbers Part 2').
checks.corrected_value: Figures unchanged. Attribution corrected: the sentence is from Ben Einstein's Bolt post 'Will Your Hardware Startup Make Money?' (blog.bolt.io/make-money/, c. 2015), not Part 2 of the series; the figures are ~10 years old and not inflation-adjusted.
checks.evidence: An independent query returned the verbatim sentence 'Simple products cost $100k-500k to develop and usually take around 6-9 months' from the Bolt post 'Will Your Hardware Startup Make Money?' (mirrored on Medium/LinkedIn, covered by TechSpot in 2015). The post's worked example (Bolt-o-Phones) has a 4-person team (ME, EE, ID, ops) spending 9 months to reach manufacturing readiness.

checks.claim: Bolt: most Chinese contract manufacturers want a ~5,000-unit MOQ and ~$1M of BOM per customer leaving the factory in the first production year.
checks.evidence: Ben Einstein's 'Hardware by the Numbers (Part 2: Financing + Manufacturing)' (Bolt blog; Medium mirror) states most Chinese CMs have a 5k-unit MOQ and that 'in the first year of production, a typical CM would like to see $1M worth of BOM leaving their factory for each customer'. Bolt's hardware glossary adds that 5,000 units for final assembly is common in China but CMs really care about total order value, and the make-money post notes many component suppliers have MOQs above 5,000 units. checks.claim: Bolt: retail price must be 2-5x manufacturing cost depending on business model.
checks.corrected_value: 2.5x-4x. Bolt's 'Hardware by the Numbers (Part 4: Retail + Exits)': 'Most consumer product MSRPs are between 2.5x and 4x of what the product costs to make' (so a $1 BOM increase can be a $4 shelf-price increase).

Bolt's make-money example uses a $32.16 BOM against a $99 price (~3.1x) and shows even that is marginal once fully loaded.

summary: 20 of 34 planned WebSearch queries completed before the session-wide budget hit 200/200; the 14 blocked queries covered the IIP-discontinuation primary source, Ultrahuman ship dates, TCB price lists, Bolt's 2-5x phrasing, SparkFun's ISED/CE split and all eight stale/missing topics, which are therefore recorded as not found or partial. Of 14 checks: 6 confirmed, 6 corrected, 1 refuted, 1 unverifiable (search budget). Load-bearing corrections: (1) the Bluetooth Declaration ID fee is $12,000 from 1 March 2026, not $11,040, and the $2,500 small-business (Innovation Incentive) discount has not existed since February 2020, which lifts the certification-stack floor from ~$10.5k to ~$15.5k (high case ~$49k, central ~$20-25k); (2) the lens's UN38.3 ($5-7k) and IEC 62133 (>$20k) inputs are the highest quotes on the market - Chinese and TUV/SGS labs quote $300-$2,000 and $1,000-$6,000 respectively - so its high case is conservative; (3) FCC TCB review-fee sources disagree ~10x ($120-$500 vs $2k-$8k) and SAR testing ($2.5k-$6k) may apply to a wrist-worn radio; (4) Bolt's $100k-$500k / 6-9-month rule is genuine but comes from the c.2015 'Will Your Hardware Startup Make Money?' post, not Part 2, and Bolt's retail multiple is 2.5-4x, not 2-5x. Bluetooth membership tiers ($0 / $3,500), Bolt's 5k MOQ / $1M-BOM norm, MarkReady's $3k-$10k module route, Upwork's $35 median and the Nordic datapoints held up; the Ultrahuman ~4-month acquisition-to-ship figure rests only on the company press release and measures finishing an already-Kickstarted ring.
